newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: WORRY OVER SAFRICA HAKE FISHING QUOTAS-I&J .
newsitem.headline: WORRY OVER SAFRICA HAKE FISHING QUOTAS-I&J .

text.p: South Africa's Irvin & Johnson Ltd (I&J) food group said on Thursday legislators should not split the deep sea hake resource between too many players or the industry would be destroyed.

I&J managing director Roy Gordon and seafoods director Charles Atkins, who addressed a parliamentary committee on the issue, told reporters after the closed-door session they were concerned that legislators did not have a full understanding of the industry.
"In order to survive in the (hake) export market, you have to achieve a sophistication of quality, and to do that, to justify the investment, you need a critical mass of quota," Atkins said.
"If you start (dividing) hake into small compartments, you're going to destroy the industry because no single person will be able to afford the kind of plant and trawlers we have," he said.
Gordon said a company could not sell to a multinational like Unilever Plc or Nestle, as I&J did, unless it had "a critical mass".

"Otherwise you can't afford the quality systems. We spent millions putting in a hazard analysis control programme which is required by the United States and Brussels. You cannot sell to those companies unless you have those systems in place," Gordon said.
South Africa's annual hake harvest is worth around 900 million rand and 49 companies have quotas.
Gordon quoted one committee member as having said rural communities had an ownership right to hake.
"The hake we catch is 200 to 300 km offshore. It's like saying the community outside Welkom has ownership rights to gold 9,000 feet down. Life isn't like that," he said.
"How we deal with transformation in industrial fisheries will not be the same as the way we deal with transformation in the inshore fisheries," Gordon said.

He said I&J was concerned that a government white paper on fisheries policy calling for marine resources to be distributed more equitably might prompt legislators to divide further quotas of industrial-species fish.

"We've always accepted that any growth in the resource would be distributed to newcomers. But what is being mooted is to take away from us, which creates an immediate loss of employment," Atkins said.
"Because of our added value processing, we create some 60 jobs per 1,000 tonnes of quota, whereas someone who justs operates a trawler creates about 20 jobs... The sea cannot accommodate everybody."
Gordon said the problems of destitute coastal fishing communities could not be solved solely through restructuring the commercial industry.
"You can't solve it purely through the fishing industry. People look at this fishing thing as the panacea to all the problems, it's not," he said.
